aliases: Problem of points and the origins of probability theory
phases: Counting for the problem of points (Pascal and Fermat, 1654)
Doctrine of chances and analytic theory (De Moivre 1718, Laplace 1812)

milestones.phase: Counting for the problem of points (Pascal and Fermat, 1654)
milestones.label: Pacioli's proportional division of stakes
milestones.work: Luca Pacioli, Summa de arithmetica, geometrica, proportioni et proportionalita, 1494
milestones.description: Early printed treatment of the interrupted game that divided the stake by rounds already won, a rule Tartaglia later criticised; neither used counting of future outcomes.

evidence.claim: Pacioli treated the interrupted game in 1494 by proportion to rounds won; Tartaglia found the rule defective.

milestones.label: Cardano's dice analysis
milestones.work: Girolamo Cardano, Liber de ludo aleae, written 1560s, printed 1663
milestones.description: Cardano counted outcomes of dice throws in the 1560s, but the text circulated only in print about a century later.

evidence.claim: Cardano's dice work dates from the 1560s and was not published until around 100 years later.

milestones.note: The 1663 printing date is stated in secondary literature; I only located a 1961 English edition record on archive.org (bookongamesofcha00card), so the printing year is not independently confirmed.

milestones.phase: Counting for the problem of points (Pascal and Fermat, 1654)
milestones.label: Pascal-Fermat correspondence solves the problem of points by counting equally likely futures
milestones.work: Pascal-Fermat letters, summer 1654
milestones.description: In five letters the two settled the division of stakes by counting the equally likely ways the game could have continued, introducing what is effectively expectation.

evidence.claim: Their correspondence of summer 1654 treated the dice problem and the problem of points.
Fermat's method counted the equally likely continuations; Pascal gave a step-by-step recursion and a binomial formula.

milestones.note: Private correspondence, so it is not the first public statement. Reclassified from first_application to precursor: it predates this event's first statement (1657) and belongs to the wider field.

milestones.label: Huygens' printed treatise on reasoning in games of chance
milestones.work: Christiaan Huygens, De ratiociniis in ludo aleae, in F. van Schooten, Exercitationum mathematicarum, 1657
milestones.description: The first published treatise devoted to probability, solving gambling problems by an expectation principle.

evidence.claim: Archive.org record dates De ratiociniis in ludo aleae to 1657.
Huygens' 1657 text is described as the first published book wholly on probability.
MacTutor reproduces the first page of De ratiociniis in ludo aleae (1657).

milestones.label: Ars conjectandi and the law of large numbers
milestones.work: Jakob Bernoulli, Ars conjectandi, Basel, 1713 (posthumous)
milestones.description: Bernoulli's posthumous book proved the first version of the law of large numbers and recast probability as a general art of conjecture.

evidence.claim: Archive.org records list the 1713 Basel edition.
Ars Conjectandi (1713) introduced the law of large numbers.

milestones.phase: Doctrine of chances and analytic theory (De Moivre 1718, Laplace 1812)
milestones.label: De Moivre's Doctrine of Chances
milestones.work: Abraham de Moivre, The Doctrine of Chances, London, 1718
milestones.description: An English textbook-style treatment extending chance calculations to games, mortality and annuities.

evidence.claim: Archive.org record dates the first edition to 1718.
De Moivre's 1718 book extended probability to more complex problems.

milestones.note: Huygens 1657 is already recorded as first_statement; De Moivre is chosen as the first systematic textbook in the later sense. This is a judgement, the claim 'first systematic treatment' is not sourced.

milestones.phase: Doctrine of chances and analytic theory (De Moivre 1718, Laplace 1812)
milestones.label: Laplace's analytic theory of probabilities
milestones.work: Pierre-Simon Laplace, Theorie analytique des probabilites, Paris, 1812
milestones.description: Laplace brought analytic methods (generating functions, asymptotics) to the subject.

evidence.claim: Archive.org record dates the Paris edition to 1812.
Laplace built on earlier work in his Theorie analytique des probabilites.

people.name: Blaise Pascal

works.whyItMatters: Founding exchange on the division of stakes; letters not printed at the time.

people.roleNote: Solved the problem of points with Fermat and developed the arithmetical triangle method

people.name: Pierre de Fermat

works.citation: Letters to Pascal on the problem of points
works.whyItMatters: Gave the enumeration argument.

people.roleNote: Counted equally likely continuations of an interrupted game

people.name: Christiaan Huygens

works.whyItMatters: First published book on probability.

people.roleNote: Wrote the first printed treatise on probability

people.name: Jakob Bernoulli

works.whyItMatters: Moved probability beyond games.

people.roleNote: Proved the first law of large numbers

works.whyItMatters: Textbook treatment of chance calculation.
Analytic methods for probability.

notes: No naming or institution milestone for the field has been established; the English Wikipedia text I read does not date the first use of the word 'probability' as a field name, and I did not search Crossref or zbMATH for 17th-century terms. The MacTutor topic page matched to this event (Mathematical games and recreations) was a poor fit and was not used. Pascal's step-by-step rule and the arithmetical triangle (1665 print) are recorded in the Pascal triangle event, not duplicated here. Cardano's printing year (1663) is taken from secondary literature only.

phases: Earlier triangles in India, Persia, China
Pascal's treatise and its use for fair division

milestones.phase: Earlier triangles in India, Persia, China
milestones.label: Triangle of binomial coefficients in China and Persia
milestones.description: The array of binomial coefficients was described long before Pascal in Indian, Persian and Chinese sources, so Pascal's contribution is a systematic treatment and use, not the table itself.

evidence.claim: The triangle is traced to Pingala/Halayudha, al-Karaji, Omar Khayyam, Jia Xian and Yang Hui.

milestones.note: Year 1010 is the Jia Xian period; the Indian sources are earlier (Pingala, Halayudha) and the Persian ones are roughly contemporary. Dates in this entry come from a secondary encyclopedia page only.

milestones.label: Stifel prints the triangle as figurate numbers
milestones.work: Michael Stifel, Arithmetica integra, Nuremberg, 1544
milestones.description: Stifel prints the table of binomial coefficients in Europe, as a table of figurate numbers.

evidence.claim: Arithmetica integra printed 1544.
Stifel described the triangle in 1544 as a table of figurate numbers; Tartaglia published six rows in 1556.

milestones.label: Pascal composes the treatise
milestones.work: Blaise Pascal, treatise on the arithmetical triangle, composed 1654, not printed until 1665
milestones.description: Pascal wrote his treatise in 1654 alongside his letters with Fermat but it remained in manuscript for years.

evidence.claim: Page images of the treatise are catalogued as 1654 in a Cambridge digital facsimile link on the Wikipedia page; print date is 1665.

milestones.note: Composition date 1654 is inferred from the facsimile caption on Wikipedia, not from a bibliographic record.

milestones.phase: Pascal's treatise and its use for fair division
milestones.label: Traite du triangle arithmetique printed
milestones.work: Blaise Pascal, Traite du triangle arithmetique, avec quelques autres petits traitez, Paris, 1665 (posthumous)
milestones.description: Pascal's systematic treatise on the triangle, with properties of the coefficients and proofs, appeared in print three years after his death.

evidence.claim: Archive.org record dates the Traite to 1665.
MacTutor calls it the most important work on the triangle and not the first to study it.

milestones.note: First systematic public treatment of the triangle, not the first appearance of the numbers.

milestones.phase: Pascal's treatise and its use for fair division
milestones.label: Using the triangle to divide stakes
milestones.work: Pascal, Traite du triangle arithmetique, 1665 (usage section)
milestones.description: Pascal applied identities of the triangle, including early explicit inductive proofs, to give a closed binomial formula for dividing the stakes.

evidence.claim: The problem of points was a main motivating example in the 1665 treatise; identities of the triangle with inductive proofs gave the formula.

milestones.note: Same printed work as the first_statement; the application dates to 1654 in the private exchange with Fermat but is recorded here at its print date.

milestones.label: Montmort calls it 'Mr. Pascal's table for combinations'
milestones.work: Pierre Remond de Montmort, Essay d'analyse sur les jeux de hazard, Paris, 1708
milestones.description: Montmort attaches Pascal's name to the triangle; de Moivre followed in 1730.

evidence.claim: Triangle named for Pascal by Montmort (1708) and de Moivre (1730).
Essay d'analyse sur les jeux de hazard, 1708.

milestones.note: Wikipedia's account of the naming was read; the passage in Montmort's book itself was not checked.

milestones.label: Edwards' monograph on the arithmetical triangle
milestones.work: A. W. F. Edwards, Pascal's Arithmetical Triangle, Griffin, 1987
milestones.description: A modern historical monograph tracing the triangle across cultures up to Pascal and after.

evidence.claim: Pascal's Arithmetical Triangle, 1987.
Wikipedia cites Edwards for the European history of the triangle.

milestones.note: Modern historical study, not the first systematic treatment (that is Pascal 1665).

people.name: Blaise Pascal

works.whyItMatters: Main source for the triangle and the induction method.

people.roleNote: Systematic treatment of the triangle and its use in probability

works.whyItMatters: Early printed European table of binomial coefficients

works.citation: Essay d'analyse sur les jeux de hazard
works.whyItMatters: Names the table for Pascal
Historical monograph

notes: The label 'technique-transfer' in the input is plausible but the real novelty is the use of the table and induction, not the numbers. The name 'Pascal's triangle' was not traced to its first user; Wikipedia says only that it is so named in much of the western world. I did not verify Pascal's Celeberrimae matheseos academiae announcement (1654), which I searched for on archive.org without a hit. Earlier-triangle dates rest on one secondary page. Thin-record pass: Wikipedia (Pascal's triangle) now read; it gives Pingala/Halayudha (India), al-Karaji, Jia Xian, Zhu Shijie 1303, Stifel 1544, Tartaglia 1556 and the naming by Montmort 1708 and de Moivre 1730. Yang Hui and Jia Xian were removed from people because no verified work record could be found; they remain named in the precursor milestone.

milestones.label: Cavalieri's indivisibles
milestones.work: Bonaventura Cavalieri, Geometria indivisibilibus, 1635
milestones.description: Wallis built his integral methods on Cavalieri's method of indivisibles and on Kepler's continuity.

evidence.claim: Wallis built on Cavalieri's indivisibles and Kepler's continuity to devise interpolation.

milestones.note: Cavalieri's year 1635 is from my background knowledge; the MacTutor page names Cavalieri but not the date.

milestones.label: Arithmetica infinitorum
milestones.work: John Wallis, Arithmetica infinitorum, in Operum mathematicorum pars altera, Oxford, 1656
milestones.description: Wallis evaluated integrals of integer powers and by interpolation reached the infinite product for pi.

evidence.claim: Archive.org record lists Wallis, Operum mathematicorum, dated 1656.
MacTutor dates Arithmetica infinitorum to 1656 and states the product for half of pi.
The Wallis product was published in 1656 and derived by interpolation.

milestones.note: Archive.org also has a 1657 catalogue record (pars prima); the 1656 date matches MacTutor and Wikipedia. I did not confirm the volume containing the Arithmetica on the item page.

milestones.label: Interpolation applied to the area of the circle
milestones.work: Wallis, Arithmetica infinitorum, 1656
milestones.description: Interpolating the series of integrals of (1-x^2)^n to fractional n to reach the quadrature of the circle yielded the product for pi.

evidence.claim: Wallis used interpolation to reach the formula; Newton later read the series by intercalation for area of circle and hyperbola.
Wallis derived the product by interpolation, not rigorous.

milestones.note: Same work as first_statement; the target problem (circle quadrature) is the point of the interpolation.

milestones.label: Interpolation introduced as a term
milestones.work: Wallis, Arithmetica infinitorum, 1656
milestones.description: MacTutor states that Wallis introduced the word interpolation in this work.

evidence.claim: MacTutor says interpolation is a word he introduced in this work.

milestones.note: Same work as first_statement.

milestones.label: Newton's binomial series builds on Wallis' interpolation
milestones.work: Isaac Newton, generalised binomial theorem, 1664-65
milestones.description: Newton cites Wallis' intercalation of series as the starting point of his own mathematics and moved from there to the general binomial series.

evidence.claim: Newton wrote that Wallis' intercalation of series was at the start of his studies.
Newton's first major discovery was the generalised binomial theorem in 1664-65.

milestones.note: Private work; see event MA65 for Newton's series.

milestones.label: Euler's Introductio and the product for sine
milestones.work: Leonhard Euler, Introductio in analysin infinitorum, Lausanne 1748
milestones.description: Euler's sine product gives a second route to Wallis' product and sets infinite products in the main line of analysis.

evidence.claim: Internet Archive scan of the 1748 Introductio.
Wikipedia notes the derivation of the product from Euler's sine product.

milestones.note: The derivation claim comes from Wikipedia; the page of the Introductio was not read.

works.whyItMatters: Source of the product and the term interpolation.
Presents the method of indivisibles on which Wallis's interpolation builds.
builds on Wallis' interpolation (per MacTutor Wallis)
infinite products and sine product

notes: Wallis' priority for the product is not disputed in the sources read. The input says 'integer-power integrals', which matches. The MacTutor topic page matched in the sources file (Analysis) is generic; the Wallis biography was used instead. Euler's later proof via the sine product is mentioned on Wikipedia but undated there and not used. I did not check Crossref or zbMATH, since no 1656 record exists there. person without verified work: Isaac Newton (developer). Thin pass 2: added Euler 1748 as a key development. Brouncker's continued fraction for 4/pi (given in Wallis' book) and Cavalieri 1635 as a bibliographic record were searched in zbMATH and archive.org without a usable record, so they are not added. Cavalieri precursor remains a history-page milestone.

canonicalName: Elliptic integrals from lemniscate and elastica (Bernoulli)

milestones.label: Jakob Bernoulli poses the elastica problem
milestones.description: Bernoulli asks for the shape of a flexible rod bent by a weight, a problem later solved with elliptic functions.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia's lemniscate-functions article says Bernoulli posed this problem in 1691.

milestones.note: Statement of the problem, not its solution by elliptic integrals.

milestones.label: Bernoulli introduces the lemniscate
milestones.work: Jakob Bernoulli, Acta Eruditorum, 1694
milestones.description: Bernoulli conceived the figure-eight curve in 1694 as a variant of the ellipse, the curve whose arc length gives the lemniscate integral.

evidence.claim: MacTutor says the lemniscate of Bernoulli was first conceived by Jakob Bernoulli in 1694.
The curve was first studied in 1694 by Jakob Bernoulli as a modification of an ellipse.
Archive.org holds the 1694 volume of the Acta Eruditorum.

milestones.note: Year of the curve is confirmed; I did not read the 1694 article, so the exact paper, the integral and any analogy with the arcsine are unverified. The input's claim that Bernoulli recognised an elliptic integral is not established by the pages read.

milestones.label: Fagnano's work on the lemniscate arc
milestones.work: Giulio Fagnano, work on the lemniscate, 1718-1723
milestones.description: Fagnano studied the arc of the lemniscate and gave the first treatment of the associated elliptic functions.

evidence.claim: The lemniscate elliptic functions were first studied by Fagnano in 1718.

milestones.label: Fagnano and Euler found the addition theorem for elliptic integrals
milestones.work: Fagnano; Euler, c. 1750
milestones.description: The sources date the first study of elliptic integrals to Fagnano and Euler around 1750.

evidence.claim: Elliptic integrals were first studied by Fagnano and Euler, c. 1750.

milestones.note: Wikipedia gives only the approximate date; no paper identified.

milestones.label: Fagnano's Produzioni matematiche
milestones.work: Giulio Carlo Fagnano, Produzioni matematiche, Pesaro, 1750
milestones.description: Collected papers, printing Fagnano's work on dividing the lemniscate and its arc.

evidence.claim: Produzioni matematiche del marchese Giulio Carlo de' Toschi di Fagnano, 1750.

milestones.note: That the lemniscate papers are in this volume is taken from the catalogue title and Wikipedia's account of Fagnano; contents were not read.

milestones.label: Legendre's Exercices de calcul intégral
milestones.work: Adrien-Marie Legendre, Exercices de calcul intégral, Paris, 1811-1817
milestones.description: Systematic treatment of elliptic integrals, reduced to three standard (Legendre) forms.

evidence.claim: Exercices de calcul intégral sur divers ordres de transcendantes, 1811.
Every elliptic integral reduces to the three Legendre canonical forms.

milestones.label: Abel's Recherches sur les fonctions elliptiques
milestones.work: N. H. Abel, Recherches sur les fonctions elliptiques, Journal fuer die reine und angewandte Mathematik 2, 1827
milestones.description: Studies the inverse functions of elliptic integrals, turning the lemniscate integral into a doubly periodic function.

evidence.claim: Crossref record, vol. 2 (1827), pp. 101-181.
Wikipedia dates Abel's work 1827-1828.

milestones.label: Jacobi's Fundamenta nova
milestones.work: C. G. J. Jacobi, Fundamenta nova theoriae functionum ellipticarum, Koenigsberg, 1829
milestones.description: Builds the theory of elliptic functions systematically from the inverse functions.

evidence.claim: Digitised record dated 1829.

works.whyItMatters: Year in which the lemniscate was conceived.
Printed his lemniscate arc work.

works.citation: Observationes de comparatione arcuum curvarum irrectificabilium (E252)
works.whyItMatters: Euler Archive entry on comparing arcs of curves, the route to his addition theorem.
Classified elliptic integrals into three standard forms.

works.citation: Recherches sur les fonctions elliptiques, Crelle 2
works.whyItMatters: Inverted elliptic integrals into elliptic functions.
First book-length theory of elliptic functions.

notes: Largely open. The elastica link: Wikipedia credits Euler (1744) and Jakob Bernoulli with elastica theory solved by elliptic functions, but no Bernoulli date for the elastica was found, so no milestone was made. The term 'lemniscate' as a coinage was not traced to a source. The first use of the name 'elliptic integral' (Legendre?) was not searched. The input summary ('treated by analogy with the arcsine') is not supported by the pages read. person without verified work: Giulio Fagnano (originator). person without verified work: Leonhard Euler (developer). Added in thin-3 pass: Bernoulli's 1691 elastica problem, Fagnano 1750, Legendre 1811, Abel 1827, Jacobi 1829. The Euler addition-theorem milestone (c.1750) is kept as found but stays low confidence; Euler's paper is listed under his entry (Euler Archive E252, 1761) without a verified date for the theorem. Six people are the schema limit. Elliptic integral naming ('integrales elliptiques', Legendre?) not traced.

canonicalName: Huygens: evolutes and the isochronous pendulum

milestones.label: Apollonius treats evolutes in Conics V
milestones.work: Apollonius, Conics, Book V (c. 200 BC)
milestones.description: Evolutes appear already in the ancient theory of normals to conics.

evidence.claim: Apollonius discussed evolutes in Book V of the Conics; Huygens is sometimes credited with first studying them (1673).

milestones.note: Date c. 200 BC from Wikipedia; not a modern general theory.

milestones.label: Pendulum clock begun
milestones.work: Huygens, pendulum regulation, from December 1656; patent 1657
milestones.description: Huygens turned to pendulum clocks in late 1656 and patented a working model in 1657, the practical aim behind the later mathematics.

evidence.claim: Interest in the freely suspended pendulum began in December 1656; working model and patent the next year.

milestones.label: Huygens' short tract Horologium
milestones.work: Christiaan Huygens, Horologium, The Hague, 1658
milestones.description: A short public description of the pendulum clock, before the cycloid and evolute theory.

evidence.claim: The design was published in a short tract titled Horologium (1658).

milestones.label: Evolute theory and isochronism of the cycloid found
milestones.work: Huygens, October 1659 onward (private)
milestones.description: Most of the book was composed in three months from October 1659; the cycloid's isochronism was first found with infinitesimal methods, and the evolute theory dates to about the same time.

evidence.claim: Book composed from October 1659; evolute theory formulated around 1659.
Huygens formulated his theory of evolutes around 1659.

milestones.note: Unpublished at the time.

milestones.label: Horologium oscillatorium printed
milestones.work: Christiaan Huygens, Horologium oscillatorium sive de motu pendulorum, Paris, 1673
milestones.description: The book defines evolutes and involutes, finds those of the cycloid and parabola, and proves the cycloid's isochronism.

evidence.claim: Archive.org records list the 1673 Paris edition.
MacTutor describes the 1673 work: evolutes and involutes defined, evolute of cycloid and parabola found.
Part III introduces the evolute as the curve unrolled.

milestones.label: Cycloidal cheeks justified by the evolute of the cycloid
milestones.work: Huygens, Horologium oscillatorium, 1673
milestones.description: Huygens used the evolute to show the thin plates in the clock's design give a cycloidal path and hence an isochronous swing.

evidence.claim: He uses evolutes to justify the cycloidal shape of the plates in Part I.

milestones.note: Same book as first_statement.

milestones.label: Jakob Bernoulli's general method for evolutes
milestones.work: Jakob Bernoulli, c. 1692
milestones.description: Bernoulli found evolutes of general curves as envelopes of circles of curvature, extending Huygens' special cases.

evidence.claim: MacTutor: a general method for evolutes as envelope of circles of curvature, and caustics around 1692.

milestones.note: Year 1692 given for the caustic work on the page; exact year of the evolute method not isolated.

milestones.label: Yoder's study of Huygens' mathematics
milestones.work: Joella G. Yoder, Unrolling Time: Christiaan Huygens and the Mathematization of Nature, Cambridge UP, 1988
milestones.description: A modern scholarly study of Huygens' route to the cycloidal pendulum and evolute theory.

evidence.claim: Unrolling Time, 1988.

milestones.note: Subject matter inferred from the title; modern study, not a first treatment.

works.whyItMatters: Source for evolute theory and isochronism of the cycloid.

works.citation: Unrolling Time: Christiaan Huygens and the Mathematization of Nature
works.whyItMatters: Modern study of Huygens' mathematics

notes: Wikipedia (Evolute) notes Apollonius treated evolutes in Conics V, so 'first' is for the modern theory. Whether Huygens coined 'evolute' was not stated by the pages read, so no naming milestone. Neither Crossref nor zbMATH records exist for 1673. The MacTutor topic page matched in the sources file (Fractal geometry) is irrelevant and was not used. Thin-record pass: Wikipedia confirms Huygens developed evolutes around 1659 from free-fall results and that the 1658 Horologium tract preceded the 1673 book. Jakob Bernoulli removed from people (no verified work); his 1692 milestone stays at low confidence. Yoder's lifespan was not found.

milestones.label: Graunt's Observations on the Bills of Mortality
milestones.work: John Graunt, Natural and Political Observations ... upon the Bills of Mortality, London, 1662
milestones.description: Graunt reworked London burial records into an estimate of survival to each age, usually called the first life table.

evidence.claim: Archive.org lists an edition dated 1662.
He is credited with the first life table; bills of mortality did not give age at death.

milestones.note: Wikipedia says copies were presented to the Royal Society on 5 February 1661, probably Old Style, i.e. 1662. Whether Graunt's 'table' is a true life table is a modern characterisation.

milestones.label: Huygens brothers interpolate Graunt's table
milestones.work: Christiaan and Lodewijk Huygens, correspondence, 1667 (unpublished)
milestones.description: The brothers distinguished mean from median lifetime and fitted a smooth curve to Graunt's table, but the exchange stayed private.

evidence.claim: Huygens correspondence of 1667 discussed Graunt's tables; unpublished.

milestones.note: Placed as precursor because it was private, although it follows Graunt in time.

milestones.label: Petty's Political Arithmetick published
milestones.work: William Petty, Political Arithmetick, London 1690 (written 1676)
milestones.description: Petty's book gives the name political arithmetic to quantitative study of population and state, the Graunt-Petty tradition.

evidence.claim: Internet Archive item titled Political Arithmetick (1676-1690).
Wikipedia describes Graunt and Petty as joint developers of early statistical and census methods.

milestones.note: 1690 is the print date; the text circulated from 1676.

milestones.label: Halley's Breslau mortality table
milestones.work: Edmond Halley, An estimate of the degrees of the mortality of mankind, Phil. Trans. 17(196), 596-610, 1693
milestones.description: Halley used actual age-at-death records for Breslau to give a better table and priced annuities.

evidence.claim: Crossref DOI 10.1098/rstl.1693.0007 gives title, Philosophical Transactions vol. 17, 1693.
MacTutor: mortality tables for Breslau published 1693, among earliest to relate mortality and age.

milestones.label: De Moivre's Annuities upon Lives
milestones.work: Abraham de Moivre, Annuities upon Lives, London 1725
milestones.description: The first mathematical treatise on life annuities builds a formula-based theory on mortality tables of Graunt and Halley.

evidence.claim: Internet Archive scan of the 1725 edition of Annuities upon Lives.

milestones.note: Role as the first systematic treatment of life contingencies is recalled from standard history and is not stated in the scan record.

works.whyItMatters: First life table.

people.roleNote: Analysed the London bills of mortality

works.citation: An estimate of the degrees of the mortality of mankind
works.whyItMatters: Table from age-at-death data.

works.citation: Petty, extract of two essays in political arithmetick (Philosophical Transactions, 1686)

First use of the term 'life table' not traced; no naming or institution milestone. The Wikipedia lead search in the sources file matched Graunt correctly. The input summary 'Halley refined it' is confirmed. Thin pass 2: added Petty 1690 and de Moivre 1725. The MacTutor page for Graunt and for Petty are 404, so their biography links stay on Wikipedia. canonicalName: Newton: infinite series and binomial theorem
aliases: De analysi per aequationes numero terminorum infinitas
Method of fluxions and infinite series

milestones.label: Wallis' interpolation of series
milestones.work: John Wallis, Arithmetica infinitorum, 1656
milestones.description: Newton started from Wallis' intercalation of series for the area of the circle and hyperbola.

evidence.claim: Newton named Wallis' intercalation of series as his starting point.

milestones.label: Newton finds the generalised binomial theorem
milestones.work: Isaac Newton, private, 1664-65
milestones.description: Newton's first major discovery was the binomial expansion for any exponent, made as a student.

evidence.claim: The generalised binomial theorem was his first major mathematical discovery, 1664-65.
Binomial series gives no proof; first results on non-integer exponents due to Newton.

milestones.note: Private work.

milestones.label: De analysi sent to Collins
milestones.work: Isaac Newton, De analysi per aequationes numero terminorum infinitas, manuscript, 1669
milestones.description: Barrow forwarded Newton's manuscript on series, quadrature and solving equations to Collins in July 1669, so the results circulated in a small circle.

evidence.claim: In July 1669 Barrow sent Newton's De Analysi to Collins.

milestones.note: Manuscript, circulated privately; it is where series are used for quadrature, but I did not read its content, so this is not recorded as first_application.

milestones.label: Wallis prints Newton's binomial series rule
milestones.work: John Wallis, A Treatise of Algebra, both Historical and Practical, London, 1685 (chapters 91-95)
milestones.description: Wallis's printed Algebra gives, with credit to Newton, the general rule for expanding a binomial to any exponent and applies it to the circle's quadrature, the first appearance of the series in print.

evidence.claim: The 1685 book credits Newton with infinite series from division and root extraction, and its contents list a chapter on his doctrine of infinite series.
evidence.source: Full-text OCR of the 1685 edition, Internet Archive item bim_early-english-books-1641-1700_a-treatise-of-algebra-_wallis-john_1685

evidence.claim: Wallis says he knows Newton's work from two letters of June and October 1676 to Oldenburg, then states the general expansion rule for a power of a binomial with a fractional or integer exponent.
evidence.source: Same 1685 text, chapters on Newton's infinite series

evidence.claim: Item date metadata gives 1685 for the book.

milestones.note: Newton's own De analysi (1669) circulated in manuscript and was printed only in 1711; his 1676 letters are private (precursors). Gregory's 1670 logarithmic version is also private. Wallis reports Newton's result secondhand; the exposition is Wallis's. Confidence is not high because no modern bibliography was checked for an earlier printed statement and the page numbers were not recorded.

milestones.label: Dissertatio de arte combinatoria
milestones.work: Gottfried Leibniz, Dissertatio de arte combinatoria, Leipzig, 1666

milestones.note: Included as the first modern formal system that explicitly claims the Leibnizian aim; the book itself was not read.

notes: Disambiguation: the Wikipedia lead matched in the sources file for this event partly concerns combinatory logic (Schonfinkel, 1920), a different subject. The title 'combinatorial logic' here refers to Leibniz' ars combinatoria, not combinatory logic. The first use of the terms 'calculus ratiocinator' and 'characteristica universalis' was not traced. The input claim that the work was largely unpublished is supported. No dated first_application. Added in thin-3 pass: Frege 1879 (Wikipedia, calculus ratiocinator), Couturat 1903 and Lewis 1918. MacTutor Leibniz confirms the 1666 Dissertatio. The undated precursor is kept with a work description only; no specific manuscript date was verified. The first use of the phrases 'calculus ratiocinator' and 'characteristica universalis' was not traced, so no naming milestone.

The 1700 'first public statement' is low confidence; identification of the item is open, and it conflicts with MacTutor's remark about Maclaurin. Leibniz' written work on determinants was not published in his lifetime beyond the two items; the later Gerhardt edition (1849-63, archive record exists) is not milestoned because I did not confirm which volume prints it. Wikipedia's Determinant page was read and gives no priority detail. person without verified work: Seki Takakazu (developer).
